strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap between weak PIT-based calibration and restrictive parametric recalibration approaches (e.g., Song et al. 2019 GPBETA), with clear articulation of why marginal PIT calibration is insufficient (error cancellation argument).

Solid theoretical foundation: the calibration-sharpness decomposition (Lemma 4.1) via generalized conditional mutual information, and the auto-calibration/sharpness-preservation guarantee for the population-level recalibration map (Proposition 5.2), are both proven rigorously in the appendix and connect cleanly to existing notions (grouping loss of Kull & Flach, proper scoring rule theory of Gneiting & Raftery).

The proposed Energy Distance Kernel reduces the cost of evaluating distributional kernels from O(n^2) to O(n log n) for real-valued targets, a practically useful and non-trivial contribution for scaling nonparametric distribution-valued regression.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many UCI datasets, four base model classes (GDN, MDN, BNN, DRF), and multiple recalibration baselines (PIT, GPBETA), with rigorous statistical testing (SKCE auto-calibration test, KS-based PIT test) rather than relying only on point-estimate calibration metrics.

Thoughtful set of supplementary analyses (comparison to conformal prediction, ablation on EDK efficiency, wall-clock comparisons, comparison to plain kernelized regression) that substantially strengthen the empirical case and demonstrate practical relevance.

Honest limitations section acknowledging the O(n_cal^3) scaling bottleneck, loss of explicit density representation, and the fact that auto-calibration is still weaker than full feature-conditional calibration.
weaknesses: The auto-calibration hypothesis test (Figure 1) has very different statistical power across datasets (explicitly noted by the authors via test-set sizes in parentheses), so acceptance/rejection rates are not directly comparable across datasets, making the headline claim that CKME 'consistently outperforms' somewhat qualitative; no correction or power-adjusted analysis is provided across the many dataset x model x method combinations.

The empirical CRPS results (Table 1, Fig. 2) show CKME sometimes substantially *worsens* predictive score relative to the uncalibrated baseline (e.g., yacht: 1.276–1.614x, housing: up to 1.19x across base models), which is in tension with the paper's theoretical claim (Proposition 5.2) that recalibration preserves sharpness; this population-level guarantee clearly does not translate cleanly to the finite-sample estimator, and this gap is not analyzed (e.g., no variance/bias study of the CKME estimator or the simplex-projection pre-image heuristic).

The distributional pre-image step is solved via a simplification (Euclidean projection to the simplex rather than the stated RKHS-weighted quadratic program in Eq. 39), justified only as an implementation convenience; the impact of this approximation on the calibration/sharpness guarantees is not empirically quantified.

Scalability remains a real concern: O(n_cal^3) complexity from kernel ridge regression is acknowledged but not mitigated (e.g., no low-rank/Nystrom approximation experiments), limiting applicability to larger calibration sets than tested here.

Kernel bandwidth (median heuristic) and only the regularization parameter are tuned; no sensitivity analysis is provided for how kernel choice/bandwidth affects calibration outcomes, which is important for a method whose entire behavior hinges on kernel design.

Remark 5.3 requires Y to be a compact metric space for the universal Gaussian-type kernel, which is not strictly satisfied by unbounded real-valued targets used throughout the experiments (e.g., UCI regression targets); this technical mismatch between assumptions and practice is not discussed.

PIT recalibration remains the strongest method for PIT-calibration (Fig. 3) and is much cheaper computationally; the paper could more directly quantify the practical trade-off (cost vs. calibration-strength gain) an end user faces when choosing CKME over the simpler, well-established PIT approach.
